alt: Average cost curves from the bakery table: average fixed cost falls from US$3.00 at 200 loaves to US$0.60 at 1,000; average variable cost and average total cost are U-shaped, and average total cost is lowest, US$2.10, at 800 loaves before rising to US$2.20.
caption: Figure: AFC falls throughout while AVC and ATC are U-shaped

alt: Total cost curves of Chipo's bakery: total fixed cost is a horizontal line at US$600; total variable cost starts at zero and reaches US$1,600 at 1,000 loaves; total cost starts at US$600 and reaches US$2,200, always exactly US$600 above total variable cost.
caption: Figure: TFC is flat, TVC starts at the origin and TC sits TFC above TVC

alt: Market demand curve for bread in Gweru plotted from the schedule: it slopes down from 8 loaves a week at US$1.60 to 20 loaves at US$0.80; a price rise from US$1.00 (17 loaves) to US$1.40 (11 loaves) is a contraction, a movement up along the same curve.
caption: Figure: the market demand curve for bread; a rise in price is a movement along it

alt: Labour market for bricklayers: demand DL slopes down and supply SL slopes up and they cross at a wage of US$14 a day with 480 workers; at US$12 there is a shortage of 150 workers (540 wanted, 390 offered) and at US$16 a surplus of 150 (570 offered, 420 wanted).
caption: Figure: the equilibrium wage is where the demand for and supply of labour cross

alt: Government budget in a worked example: revenue of US$5,100 million (income tax 2,400, VAT 1,800, customs and excise 600, other 300) against spending of US$5,700 million (education 1,500, infrastructure 1,100, health 900, social protection 650, other 650, defence 500, interest 400), giving a budget deficit of US$600 million.
caption: Figure: spending of US$5,700 million is above revenue of US$5,100 million, a deficit of US$600 million

alt: Revenue per unit for the car wash: the average revenue (price) curve falls from US$12 for 1 wash to US$7 for 6, and marginal revenue falls faster, from US$12 to US$2, so MR is below AR after the first unit; at 4 washes AR is US$9 and MR is US$6.
caption: Figure: when a firm must cut its price to sell more, marginal revenue lies below average revenue

alt: Demand for chicken shifts right from D1 to D2 after a pay rise: at every price 150 kg a week more is demanded, for example at US$5 quantity demanded rises from 300 kg to 450 kg, an increase in demand.
caption: Figure: a pay rise shifts demand for chicken right, from D1 to D2

alt: Circular flow of income as a schematic: firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit to households for the factors of production (income, on one side), and households spend their income on the goods and services firms produce (spending, on the other), so output, income and expenditure measure the same flow and give the same total.
caption: Figure: schematic of the circular flow; output, income and expenditure are the same flow measured at different points

alt: Production possibility lines for the same resources: Country A (maize 60 tonnes or cloth 30 thousand metres) has a flatter line than Country B (maize 20 or cloth 20), so A's opportunity cost of 1 tonne of maize is 0.5 thousand metres of cloth against B's 1; A has the comparative advantage in maize and B in cloth, and specialising lifts total maize from 40 to 50 tonnes with cloth unchanged at 25.
caption: Figure: the flatter line shows the lower opportunity cost of maize, so Country A specialises in maize and Country B in cloth

alt: Credit creation with a 20 percent reserve ratio: a US$5,000 deposit in Bank A is split into 1,000 kept and 4,000 lent; the 4,000 becomes Bank B's deposit (800 kept, 3,200 lent), then Bank C 3,200 (640 and 2,560), then Bank D 2,560 (512 and 2,048); total deposits after four banks are 14,760 and the maximum is 5,000 divided by 0.2, which is US$25,000.
caption: Figure: each bank keeps 20% as reserves and lends the rest, so every new deposit is 80% of the last

alt: Current account of a fictional country in US$ million: goods balance -900, services -250, primary income -550 and secondary income +1,200 add up to a current account deficit of 500; the large remittances in secondary income reduce the deficit but do not remove it.
caption: Figure: the four balances add up to the current account balance (negative bars are deficits)

alt: Two aggregate demand and supply sketches: in demand-pull inflation the AD curve shifts right near full capacity, so the price level rises a lot while output rises only a little; in cost-push inflation the AS curve shifts left, so the price level rises and output falls.
caption: Figure: demand-pull inflation comes from a shift of AD to the right; cost-push from a shift of AS to the left

alt: Four comparisons of two fictional countries: Country A has the higher real GDP per head (US$4,200 against US$2,400) but Country B has longer life expectancy (71 against 58 years), more schooling (9.4 against 5.1 years) and a higher HDI (0.684 against 0.561), so income alone ranks them the wrong way round for welfare.
caption: Figure: Country A has the higher income per head, but Country B does better on health, education and the HDI

alt: Output of a furniture workshop with five carpenters: when each makes whole chairs the output is 15 chairs a day (3 per worker), and after dividing the work into cutting, shaping, joining, sanding and finishing it is 24 chairs a day (4.8 per worker), a rise of 60 percent with the same workers.
caption: Figure: dividing the work raised the workshop's output from 15 to 24 chairs a day

alt: A subsidy of US$10 a bag shifts the supply of fertiliser right from S1 to S2: the price farmers pay falls from US$30 to US$24 and the quantity rises from 2,800 to 3,280 bags a month; the cost to the government is 10 x 3,280 = US$32,800.
caption: Figure: a subsidy shifts supply right; price falls and quantity rises

alt: Street lighting for 60 traders: it is worth 60 x 55 = US$3,300 a year to them and costs US$2,400, so it should be provided, but if only 25 traders pay US$40 each the firm collects US$1,000, far below the cost, because the others free ride.
caption: Figure: the lighting is worth more than it costs, but free riders leave the firm with less than half the cost

alt: Ladder of economic integration, each step adding to the one below: preferential trade area (reduced tariffs between members), free trade area (tariffs removed), customs union (plus a common external tariff), common market (plus free movement of labour and capital) and economic and monetary union (plus common economic policies or a common currency).
caption: Figure: the five forms of economic integration, each adding one feature to the step before (schematic of the lesson's table)

alt: Chain of effects of a rise in interest rates using the lesson's numbers: loan rates rise from 8 to 12 percent so interest on a US$10,000 loan rises from US$800 to US$1,200 a year and savings rates rise from 4 to 7 percent so US$5,000 earns US$350 instead of US$200; firms cut investment and households spend less, aggregate demand falls and pressure on prices eases.
caption: Figure: how a rise in interest rates works through spending to lower inflation pressure (a flow, using the worked example's numbers)

alt: Foreign exchange market for the kora: higher export demand shifts demand right from D1 to D2, so at 4 US cents there is excess demand of 200 million kora and the price of the kora rises to 5 cents with 800 million traded, an appreciation of 25 percent (US$1 = 25 kora becomes US$1 = 20 kora).
caption: Figure: a rise in export demand shifts the demand for a currency right and it appreciates

alt: Total daily cost against the daily wage for two methods: labour-intensive (60 workers plus US$200 of machinery) costs 60w + 200 and capital-intensive (15 workers plus US$680) costs 15w + 680; at a wage of US$12 they cost 920 and 860 so capital is cheaper, at US$8 they cost 680 and 800 so labour is cheaper, and the costs are equal at about US$10.67.
caption: Figure: below a wage of about US$10.67 the labour-intensive method is cheaper; above it the capital-intensive method is

alt: Long-run average cost curve from the five plant sizes: average cost falls from US$20 at 1,000 units to US$10 at 10,000 units (economies of scale), then rises to US$11 at 12,000 units (diseconomies of scale), so the most efficient scale is 10,000 units.
caption: Figure: the long-run average cost curve falls, reaches a minimum, then rises

alt: Supply of maize shifts left from S1 to S2 in a drought: at every price 300 tonnes less is supplied, for example at US$300 quantity supplied falls from 1,200 to 900 tonnes, a decrease in supply of 25 percent.
caption: Figure: a drought shifts the supply of maize left, from S1 to S2

alt: Maize meal market with a maximum price of US$7, below the equilibrium of US$9 and 1,100 bags: at US$7 only 900 bags are supplied but 1,300 are demanded, a shortage of 400 bags a week.
caption: Figure: a maximum price below equilibrium creates a shortage

alt: Wheat market with a minimum price of US$350 a tonne, above the equilibrium of US$320 and 640 tonnes: at US$350 farmers supply 700 tonnes but only 550 tonnes are demanded, a surplus of 150 tonnes a month.
caption: Figure: a minimum price above equilibrium creates a surplus

alt: Demand for cement from the single supplier slopes down; with a cost of US$110 a tonne the profit-maximising point is US$150 and 9,000 tonnes, giving abnormal profit of 40 x 9,000 = US$360,000 a month, while a competitive market would charge US$110 and sell 14,000 tonnes.
caption: Figure: a monopoly restricts output and charges more than a competitive market would

alt: Monopoly cost and revenue curves from the table: marginal revenue (46, 38, 30, 22, 14, 6) is above marginal cost (20, 14, 12, 14, 18, 24) up to the 4th unit, so output is 4 units; the price is read up to the demand curve (AR) at US$34, average total cost is US$25, and abnormal profit is (34 - 25) x 4 = US$36.
caption: Figure: the monopoly produces where MR = MC (4 units) but charges the price on the demand curve, US$34

alt: Country X GDP: nominal GDP rises from US$48,000 million in 2025 to US$54,000 million in 2026 (12.5 percent) but real GDP in 2025 prices rises only from 48,000 to 49,090.9 million (2.3 percent), because prices rose 10 percent.
caption: Figure: most of the rise in nominal GDP is higher prices; real GDP grew far less

alt: Occupational distribution of 5,250 thousand workers in a fictional country: 60.0 percent in the primary sector (3,150 thousand), 12.0 percent in the secondary sector (630 thousand) and 28.0 percent in the tertiary sector (1,470 thousand), typical of a developing economy.
caption: Figure: most workers are in the primary sector, as in a typical developing economy

alt: Five demand curve shapes for price elasticity of demand: PED 0 is a vertical line, between 0 and 1 a steep line, exactly 1 a curve bending to both axes with price times quantity constant, above 1 a gentle line, and infinity a horizontal line.
caption: Figure: the shape of the demand curve for each value of PED, drawn on the same scale

alt: Demand for screen repairs is elastic: when the price is cut from US$10 to US$8, weekly repairs rise from 100 to 150; the revenue lost on existing sales is 200 dollars (2 x 100) but the revenue gained on extra sales is 400 dollars (8 x 50), so total revenue rises from US$1,000 to US$1,200.
caption: Figure: revenue gained (green) and lost (amber) when an elastic price is cut

alt: Cost curves for a firm in perfect competition: the price is US$24 so marginal revenue is 24; marginal cost (20, 14, 11, 11, 14, 26) is below 24 up to the 5th batch and above it for the 6th, so output is 5 batches; average total cost at 5 batches is US$20, so the firm earns abnormal profit of (24 - 20) x 5 = US$20 a day.
caption: Figure: the firm produces where MC meets the price line, and profit is the gap between price and ATC times output

alt: Three parallel straight supply curves: S1 cuts the quantity axis and is price inelastic (PES less than 1), S2 passes through the origin and has PES exactly 1, S3 cuts the price axis and is price elastic (PES greater than 1).
caption: Figure: where a straight supply curve meets the axes tells you its elasticity

alt: Two illustrative population pyramids: the young population has a wide base, 40 percent aged 0 to 14, narrowing quickly to 5 percent aged 60 and over, while the older population has straighter sides, 17 percent aged 0 to 14 and 16 percent aged 60 and over.
caption: Figure: a wide base means a young, fast-growing population; straighter sides mean an older, slow-growing one

alt: Production possibility curve of Country X, consumer goods against capital goods: points A to F lie on the curve from 50 thousand capital goods to 100 thousand consumer goods; G (40, 30) lies inside the curve so resources are unused, and H (60, 44) lies outside so it is unattainable.
caption: Figure: Country X's PPC with points on, inside and beyond the curve

alt: Production possibility curves before and after investment and training: PPC1 runs from 80 thousand units of clothing to 40 thousand tonnes of food, PPC2 lies outside it from 100 units of clothing to 50 thousand tonnes of food, so the combination of 40 thousand tonnes of food and 50 thousand units of clothing, impossible before, is now attainable.
caption: Figure: an outward shift from PPC1 to PPC2 makes new combinations attainable

alt: Three production possibility curves for food and clothing with the same end points, 80 thousand units of clothing or 40 thousand tonnes of food: the straight line loses 20 thousand units of clothing for every 10 thousand tonnes of food, the concave curve loses 4, 10, 20 then 46 (rising cost) and the convex curve loses 34, 24, 14 then 8 (falling cost).
caption: Figure: straight-line, concave and convex PPCs through the same end points

alt: Average tax rate against monthly income for a banded income tax (first US$300 free, 20 percent up to US$1,000, 30 percent above): it rises from 12.5 percent at US$800 to 22.0 percent at US$2,000, so the tax is progressive, whereas a proportional tax stays at a flat rate.
caption: Figure: under a progressive tax the average rate rises with income; a proportional tax stays flat

alt: Cooking oil with an import quota of 200 thousand litres: the supply available to the market is local supply plus the quota, which meets demand at US$1.60, where consumers buy 600, local firms supply 400 and imports fill the 200 gap; the price is higher than with the 0.40 tariff and the government collects no revenue.
caption: Figure: a quota limits imports to 200 thousand litres and the price rises to US$1.60

alt: School shoes market: demand rises from D1 to D2 in January; at the old price of US$25 quantity demanded is 700 but only 500 are supplied, a shortage of 200, so the equilibrium moves to US$30 and 600 pairs a week.
caption: Figure: an increase in demand raises both the equilibrium price and quantity

alt: Smelter example: each extra batch earns US$900; extra private cost (500, 600, 700, 850, 950) stays below 900 up to the 4th batch, so the firm produces 4, but extra social cost (private plus US$250 external cost) stays below 900 only up to the 2nd batch, so the best output for society is 2 batches.
caption: Figure: the firm compares revenue with private cost; society should compare it with social cost

alt: A tax of US$0.50 a bottle shifts supply left from S1 to S2: the price paid by consumers rises from US$2.00 to US$2.30 and quantity falls from 1,400 to 1,160 bottles; producers keep US$1.80 and the tax revenue rectangle is 0.50 x 1,160 = US$580 a day.
caption: Figure: a specific tax shifts supply up by the tax; price rises and quantity falls

alt: Cooking oil market: at the world price of US$1.00 local firms supply 100 and consumers demand 900 thousand litres, so imports are 800; a US$0.40 tariff lifts the price to US$1.40, local supply rises to 300, demand falls to 700, imports fall to 400 thousand litres and the government collects US$160,000 a week.
caption: Figure: a tariff raises the price, cuts imports and raises local output and government revenue

alt: Price indices (2023 = 100): export prices 100, 104, 98, 112 and import prices 100, 108, 112, 105 give terms of trade of 100, 96.3, 87.5, 106.7 for 2023 to 2026; they fall below 100 in 2024 and 2025 (unfavourable) and recover to 106.7 in 2026 (favourable).
caption: Figure: the terms of trade are the export price index divided by the import price index, times 100

alt: Demand and supply diagram for the tomato market: the downward demand curve D and upward supply curve S cross at a price of US$8 and 600 crates a day; at US$4 the gap between 300 crates supplied and 900 demanded is a shortage of 600.
caption: Figure: the tomato market finds its equilibrium at US$8 and 600 crates

alt: Market supply curve for tomatoes: it slopes up from 30 crates a week at US$4 to 87 crates at US$10; a price rise from US$6 (51 crates) to US$10 (87 crates) is an extension, a movement up along the same curve.
caption: Figure: the market supply curve for tomatoes; a rise in price is a movement along it

alt: Stacked bars of unemployment in a farming district with a labour force of 200 thousand: frictional (6 thousand) and structural (14 thousand) stay the same every quarter, while seasonal unemployment is 4, 2, 15 and 9 thousand, so the total is 24, 22, 35 and 29 thousand, a rate of 12.0, 11.0, 17.5 and 14.5 percent, highest in July to September.
caption: Figure: only the seasonal part of unemployment changes through the year; frictional and structural stay at 20 thousand

alt: Value added along a cotton-to-shirt chain: the farmer adds 120, the ginnery 80, the mill 140, the clothing factory 220 and the retailer 140; each bar rises from the cost of inputs to the value of output and the total value added is 700, the price consumers pay for the shirts.
caption: Figure: value is added at every stage, and the parts add up to the final price of US$700

alt: Average monthly earnings in five jobs: farm hand 150, machine operator 320, electrician 640, bank teller 450 and doctor 1,200 US dollars; the skilled job earns most in each sector, and the doctor earns 8 times the farm hand.
caption: Figure: pay rises with skill within each sector, and the doctor earns 8 times as much as the farm hand

alt: Number line of cross elasticity of demand: negative values mean complements and positive values mean substitutes; kombi and bus rides at +0.5 are weak substitutes and cars and petrol at −0.5 are complements.
caption: Figure: where the two worked examples fall on the cross elasticity scale (schematic scale, values from the examples)

alt: Number line of income elasticity of demand: negative values (inferior goods) lie below 0, values between 0 and 1 are normal necessities, values above 1 are luxuries; beef at +1.2 is a luxury and the cheapest maize meal at −0.4 is an inferior good.
caption: Figure: where the two worked examples fall on the income elasticity scale (schematic scale, values from the examples)
